Long case 07 · General Surgery

Liver Secondaries

The case where the two Indian textbooks and Bailey & Love disagree about something that matters enormously to the patient: whether this is a palliative situation or a curable one. Learn the modern position and the reason for it, because the older teaching writes off people who can now be cured.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The case in one breath

How common, and how often
Colorectal cancer is worldwide the third most common solid organ malignancy and the fourth most common cause of cancer-related death. Up to 70% of patients with colorectal cancer develop liver metastases: synchronous in 15 to 25% and metachronous in 20 to 45%.​B&L 69 · p.1216
Synchronous and metachronous, defined
SRB: synchronous means primary and secondaries identified at the same time, as with carcinoma stomach; metachronous means the secondaries develop much later, possibly long after treatment of the primary, as with melanoma and breast carcinoma.​SRB 11 · p.605
Why the liver
SRB's four routes, which is the cleanest way to organise the primary search: direct spread from stomach, colon, gallbladder and bile ducts; hepatic artery, classically melanoma; portal vein, carcinoid and other gastrointestinal malignancies; and lymphatics, breast and lung.​SRB 11 · p.605 S Das says the same more briefly: metastasis from the gastrointestinal tract via the portal vein, or from organs like the breast through lymphatics.​Das 35 · p.524
And how the figures have moved
"Thirty years ago, metastatic CRC was associated with a 5-year survival of less than 3%; however, liver resection in selected patients with liver-only metastatic disease demonstrated 5-year survivals of 50%."​B&L 69 · p.1216 That single sentence is why this case is no longer automatically a palliative one, and it is the sentence to open with.
The numbers that frame every answer in this case Only 20% of patients are candidates for resection at presentation. A further 20 to 30% become operable following chemotherapy. After resection, 5-year overall survival is 50%, but tumour recurs in 65%, and in 40% of those the recurrence is limited to the liver.​B&L 69 · p.1216

So: a fifth are operable now, another quarter can be made operable, half of those operated on are alive at five years, and most recurrences are again confined to the liver, which is why re-resection is a real option.

2Palliative or curable? The disagreement that defines the case

Is the treatment of choice chemotherapy or resection? SRB 11 p.605 says chemotherapy is the treatment of choice; B&L 69 p.1216 says resection is the only potentially curative option
SRB
"Chemotherapy is the treatment of choice. Surgery has a definitive role if primary is from the colon, kidney." If the primary is in the colon a palliative hemicolectomy is done, and "along with that if a solitary secondary in the liver is present, it can be resected. If secondaries are in single lobe, hemihepatectomy is done."​SRB 11 · p.605 So surgery is positioned as an adjunct for a solitary or unilobar deposit.
Bailey & Love 28e
The reverse: "Despite recent advances in chemotherapeutic agents, resection remains the only potentially curative option, but only 20% of patients will be candidates at presentation. A further 20–30% will become operable following chemotherapy."​B&L 69 · p.1216 Chemotherapy's main role in its account is to downstage disease into operability, not to be the definitive treatment: advances in oncology have "increased the ability of chemotherapy to 'downstage' disease sufficiently to operable lesions that would have been formerly considered inoperable".​B&L 69 · p.1210
Live and consequential disagreement, and here you should take Bailey & Love's side, because the question is not one of opinion but of what cures people. Answer in this order, which concedes SRB's realism without accepting its conclusion:

"Resection is the only potentially curative treatment: five-year survival after resection of liver-only colorectal metastases is about 50%, against under 3% for untreated metastatic disease. Only about 20% are resectable at presentation, and chemotherapy's most important role is to downstage another 20–30% into operability. So my first question is not which chemotherapy, but whether this patient can be made resectable."​B&L 69 · p.1210, p.1216

Then concede the part of SRB that is true: most patients are not resectable, and for them chemotherapy is the treatment, and if the colonic primary is obstructing it still needs dealing with.​SRB 11 · p.605 The error to avoid is treating "liver secondaries" as a single prognostic category. Liver-only metastatic colorectal cancer is a potentially curable disease and should be referred to a hepatobiliary unit, not palliated.
What makes liver metastases irresectable? SRB 11 p.605 selects on number, size and segments; B&L 69 p.1216 says those criteria have been abandoned
SRB's criteria for selecting a patient for liver resection
Stage of the primary; number of secondaries; type of primary resection; segments involved; size of the largest liver lesion; and associated liver disease such as secondary cirrhosis.​SRB 11 · p.605 These are essentially the older, count-and-measure criteria.
Bailey & Love 28e, naming those criteria as historical
"Previously, patients with synchronous metastases, a rectal primary, multiple diffuse metastases, metastases larger than 5 cm, disease-free intervals of less than 1 year from the diagnosis of primary disease or a high serum CEA were considered irresectable and suitable only for palliative treatment. Modern surgical techniques and chemotherapy regimes now mean that resection with curative intent is defined as the ability to successfully remove all residual disease from the liver with clear surgical margins, leaving adequate disease-free viable liver. Technical contraindications to resection are related to the anatomical location of metastases, principally the involvement of major vascular or biliary structures."​B&L 69 · p.1216
And on extrahepatic disease
"Historically, extrahepatic metastatic disease was considered a contraindication to liver surgery, but long-term survival is now possible in selected patients. Survival after lung resection for colorectal metastases is similar to that seen after liver resection, 40 to 50%, with low morbidity and mortality."​B&L 69 · p.1217
Live disagreement, and the modern criterion is functional rather than numerical, which is the single most important thing to be able to say in this case.

Answer: "Resectability is no longer defined by the number or the size of the deposits. It is defined by whether all disease can be removed with clear margins while leaving enough viable, disease-free liver behind. The technical contraindications are anatomical: involvement of major vascular or biliary structures. Multiple metastases, a deposit over 5 cm, synchronous disease, a rectal primary, a short disease-free interval and a high CEA were all once considered contraindications and are not now."​B&L 69 · p.1216

Then add the volume rule, which is what "enough liver" means: a future liver remnant of at least 25% of total estimated liver volume in a normal liver, and 40% in the presence of cirrhosis,​B&L 69 · p.1212, p.1217 and note that where the remnant is too small it can be grown by portal vein embolisation rather than the patient being declared inoperable. SRB's criteria are still worth knowing, because the factors it lists do predict prognosis; they just no longer decide operability.

3History: find the primary, and date it

Have you ever had an operation for cancer? When, and for what? Why firstBecause it may settle the whole case in one answer. SRB lists it explicitly among the features: history of earlier surgery, like mastectomy or wide excision of a melanoma.​SRB 11 · p.605
And date it, because the interval mattersA long interval suggests a metachronous deposit, classically from melanoma or breast carcinoma.​SRB 11 · p.605 A short interval or simultaneous discovery is synchronous disease.
Edition note worth carryingA disease-free interval of less than one year was once a reason to call the disease irresectable, and is no longer.​B&L 69 · p.1216 So do not use the interval to write the patient off; use it to understand the biology.
Any change in bowel habit, blood in the stool, or tenesmus? Rules inA colorectal primary, which is the one worth finding because it is the one with a 50% five-year survival after liver resection.​B&L 69 · p.1216 SRB's colonic pointers: constipation or diarrhoea, a palpable mass, features of obstruction.​SRB 11 · p.605
SoIf you find nothing else in the history, find this. A colorectal primary changes the case from palliative to potentially curative.
Any vomiting, early fullness, weight loss? Any jaundice, itching, pale fatty stools? DistinguishesSRB's organ-by-organ checklist, which is the most efficient way to search for a primary at the bedside:​SRB 11 · p.605
StomachVomiting, visible gastric peristalsis, a palpable stomach mass.
PancreasJaundice, steatorrhoea, itching, a palpable gallbladder.
ColonAltered bowels, a palpable mass, obstruction.
TestisFullness, a hard mass, loss of testicular sensation.
SoRun those four and you will have covered most primaries that metastasise to the liver, and the testicular one is the question nobody asks.
Is there pain over the liver? What kind? Why the character mattersSRB gives the mechanism: pain in liver secondaries is due to stretching of the liver capsule or to tumour necrosis, and "often pain may be of the primary tumour".​SRB 11 · p.605
SoCapsular pain is a dull right hypochondrial ache worsened by movement; it tells you the deposits are large or peripheral, not that they are inoperable. And if the pain is elsewhere, it may be the primary speaking.
Any fever, and any past dysentery? Rules out, which is the point of askingThe main differentials for a nodular liver in India are infective, not malignant. S Das's amoebic picture: a patient who had amoebic dysentery months or years ago, now with pain in the right hypochondrium referred to the right shoulder and fever, looking pale and slightly icteric, with a palpable and very tender liver, and intercostal tenderness even if the liver is not palpable; the upper limit of liver dullness is raised.​Das 35 · p.523
And how it is confirmedEntamoeba histolytica in the stool is diagnostic, and aspiration of anchovy sauce, chocolate-coloured pus leaves no doubt about the diagnosis.​Das 35 · p.523 SRB adds the chronic form: a smooth, firm or hard, non-tender palpable liver without acute features.​SRB 11 · p.590 That is the one that can be mistaken for secondaries.
And the other mimicsSRB's differential for liver secondaries: multicentric hepatoma; macronodular cirrhosis; polycystic liver disease; hydatid cyst of the liver.​SRB 11 · p.605
Any urticaria, or contact with dogs and sheep? Rules in a mimic you must not biopsyHydatid cyst. S Das: when it lies near the lower margin of the liver it gives a palpable spherical and smooth swelling with hydatid thrill and fluctuation, diagnosed by a history of urticaria, eosinophilia, the complement fixation test and Casoni's intradermal reaction.​Das 35 · p.524
Why it matters so much hereSRB lists hydatid disease as a contraindication to liver biopsy, because it will precipitate anaphylaxis,​SRB 11 · p.586 along with haemangioma, bleeding disorders and ascites. A needle into the wrong liver lesion can kill the patient, so this question is not academic.

4Examination, and what each finding settles

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.

For the abdomen, privacy is part of the examination B&L asks for permission to begin the consultation in ensured privacy, and notes that "if a patient is still uncomfortable or reticent, the presence of a close family member as a chaperone can help. A tense patient without a relaxed abdominal wall will substantively affect the accuracy of the clinical examination."​B&L 63 · p.1051 So this is not only manners: an embarrassed patient guards, and a guarded abdomen hides the sign you are after.

First, prove the mass is liver

Does it move with respiration, is it continuous with the liver dullness, and can you move it sideways? Rules inS Das: "Hepatic swellings are continuous with the liver dullness and move up and down with respiration. It is difficult to move the swellings sideways."​Das 35 · p.523 Enlargement is established by palpating the lower border and percussing the upper limit, and the upper limit is the half everyone forgets, so a pushed-up liver is mistaken for hepatomegaly.
DistinguishesSwellings of liver, gallbladder, stomach and spleen move well with respiration; a renal or suprarenal swelling moves very little.​Das 35 · p.518, p.519 And the movement is up and down, which must not be confused with the anteroposterior movement of the abdominal wall during breathing.​Das 35 · p.519
And percuss the loinS Das's test, just outside the erector spinae, where the area is normally resonant: a liver or splenic swelling is dull on percussion, whereas a renal swelling is resonant,​Das 35 · p.521 because a retroperitoneal organ keeps bowel in front of it.

Then characterise the liver

The description that makes the diagnosis, and all three books agree Multiple, hard, nodular, with umbilication of the nodules due to central necrosis.​SRB 11 · p.605 S Das: the liver is "enlarged, irregular with nodules of varying size and shape and becomes hard. The nodules may show softening in the centre and may become umbilicated."​Das 35 · p.524 SRB's summary box: poor general condition; a palpable liver which is hard, multinodular with umbilication; clinical features of the primary; ascites plus or minus; jaundice plus or minus.​SRB 11 · p.605

So the four words to say are hard, nodular, umbilicated, and the primary. And know the mechanism of umbilication, which is central necrosis of a nodule that has outgrown its blood supply.
Jaundice
Present or absent, and SRB gives the determinant: jaundice depends on the extent of liver involvement.​SRB 11 · p.605 S Das: the patient "may be jaundiced sooner or later".​Das 35 · p.524 So its absence does not mean limited disease, and its presence does not mean inoperable disease: it may be the primary obstructing the bile duct.
Ascites
Present or absent. Its presence suggests peritoneal disease, which CT is poor at detecting: B&L notes CT is used for staging and resectability "apart from peritoneal metastases".​B&L 69 · p.1196 So clinical ascites adds information that imaging may miss, and it is the finding that most often moves a patient from operable to inoperable.
The signs of the primary, deliberately sought
SRB's list to examine for: rectovesical secondaries, the Blumer shelf, on rectal examination; and supraclavicular lymph node enlargement, Virchow's node, that is Troisier's sign.​SRB 11 · p.605 Both are free, both are often skipped, and either settles the diagnosis.
Poor general condition
SRB lists it first among the clinical features.​SRB 11 · p.605 It matters because it is one of the things that will decide whether a major hepatectomy is survivable.
One benign thing that fools people Riedel's lobe: a congenital tongue-shaped projection from the lower border of the right lobe. S Das: "It is likely to be mistaken for an enlarged gallbladder but it is more wide and flat than the gallbladder and lacks the spherical outline of the distended gallbladder."​Das 35 · p.523 Wide and flat, not spherical: that is the distinction.

5Investigations, and why each one

Find the primary first

How SRB says to look
"Primary is identified by gastroscopy, colonoscopy, contrast X-rays, CT scan."​SRB 11 · p.605 In a patient with liver secondaries and no obvious primary, those four cover most of it.
Tumour marker
CEA.​SRB 11 · p.605 And note the edition point: a high serum CEA was once a criterion of irresectability and is no longer.​B&L 69 · p.1216 Use it as a baseline and for follow-up, not as a reason to decline surgery.
Liver function tests
On SRB's list,​SRB 11 · p.605 and they matter for assessing whether the remnant liver will cope.

Image the liver

Ultrasound first
SRB: multiple hypo- or hyperechoic lesions; the site of a possible primary; nodal status; ascites.​SRB 11 · p.605 Four questions from one cheap test.
CT, and its one blind spot
Used for assessing stage and resectability of liver tumours apart from peritoneal metastases.​B&L 69 · p.1196 Hold on to that exception: CT is the staging workhorse but it under-detects peritoneal disease.
MRI, which is better for the liver itself
"Magnetic resonance of the liver is superior to CT in characterising focal lesions. The resolution for small metastases is superior and is further improved by liver-specific" contrast agents.​B&L 69 · p.1196 So CT stages the patient and MRI counts and characterises the liver lesions.
PET, for what it adds
B&L's indications: to quantify tumour spread, and to help differentiate.​B&L 69 · p.1197
The full staging package, as B&L specifies it
"A specialist multidisciplinary team should coordinate the staging of patients with colorectal liver metastases and the treatment plan. Routine staging involves triple-phase CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, contrast MRI scan of the liver, whole-body PET-CT to identify metastatic disease, with or without laparoscopy and intraoperative ultrasonography."​B&L 69 · p.1217 Learn that list as one sentence; it is the most quotable thing in the chapter.
Laparoscopy with laparoscopic ultrasound
SRB: "very useful to detect small secondaries".​SRB 11 · p.605 It is how the peritoneal disease that CT missed gets found, before a laparotomy is wasted.
Should you biopsy the liver lesion? SRB 11 p.605 says only if the primary cannot be found; B&L 69 p.1216 says avoid it if resection is contemplated
SRB
"Liver biopsy is done, only if primary is not identified by any of these methods."​SRB 11 · p.605 Elsewhere it gives the indications for liver biopsy as advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and selected liver secondaries where the primary is not detected, with the needle a Vim-Silverman or, better, a Menghini, usually through the right mid-axillary line. Complications: haemorrhage, infection, bile leak and biliary peritonitis. Contraindications: hydatid disease, because it will precipitate anaphylaxis; haemangioma; bleeding disorders; ascites.​SRB 11 · p.586
Bailey & Love 28e
For intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, where resection is being considered, it is explicit: "If surgical resection is considered, biopsy should be avoided; in borderline cases diagnostic laparoscopy and intraoperative ultrasonography will exclude additional hepatic or peritoneal disease."​B&L 69 · p.1216 The same principle it applies to resectable pancreatic tumours, where percutaneous transperitoneal biopsy "should be avoided as far as possible".​B&L 72 · p.1283
These are compatible, and saying how is the answer: biopsy is for patients you are not going to operate on.

Answer: "I would not biopsy a liver lesion I intend to resect, because of the risk of tract seeding and because it rarely changes the plan; diagnostic laparoscopy with intraoperative ultrasound is the better way to resolve doubt. I would biopsy when the primary cannot be found and the histology will direct chemotherapy, or when the disease is clearly unresectable and I need tissue before palliative treatment."

Then give the two safety points, which are SRB's and are the bits examiners like: exclude hydatid disease before putting a needle into any liver lesion, because biopsy will precipitate anaphylaxis, and avoid biopsy in haemangioma, bleeding disorders and ascites.​SRB 11 · p.586 A patient with urticaria, eosinophilia and a smooth spherical cystic liver swelling needs serology, not a needle.​Das 35 · p.524

6Treatment, and the reasoning behind each choice

The anatomy you must have before you discuss any resection The liver divides at Cantlie's line: segments V to VIII to its right are supplied by the right hepatic artery and right portal vein and drain via the right hepatic duct; segments I to IV to its left by the left hepatic artery and left portal vein, draining via the left hepatic duct.​B&L 69 · p.1193 Each segment is drained by a hepatic vein tributary, and "this concept facilitates anatomical liver resection".​B&L 69 · p.1193 So resections of individual segments, of the whole left or right hemiliver, or combinations, are all possible, which is precisely why a count of deposits no longer decides operability.

Making an inoperable liver operable

The four tools
B&L: advances in surgery and anaesthesia, "including combinations of staged procedures, portal vein embolisation, ablation and local resections, increased the number of potentially curative procedures", while oncology increased the ability of chemotherapy to downstage.​B&L 69 · p.1210 Name all four when asked how you would make a patient resectable.
Portal vein embolisation, and the numbers
"Preoperative PVE induces hypertrophy of one side of the liver prior to a planned resection of the other side."​B&L 69 · p.1211 Embolising one side causes hypertrophy of the contralateral segments and so increases the size of the proposed future liver remnant.​B&L 69 · p.1212
The threshold"There is no clear consensus about the volume required for adequate postresection liver function but an FLR to total estimated liver volume ratio of at least 25% is recommended with a normal liver and 40% in the presence of cirrhosis."​B&L 69 · p.1212 And in the colorectal metastasis section: "An FLR of 25% of preoperative volume is considered sufficient to prevent postoperative hepatic failure."​B&L 69 · p.1217
Materials, if pressedPolyvinyl alcohol particles, coils, gelatin sponge, n-butyl cyanoacrylate and lipiodol, or fibrin glue.​B&L 69 · p.1212
Staged resection
Extensive resection of the liver in two stages.​B&L 69 · p.1211
The Makuuchi eponym belongs to the entry above, not this one B&L attaches it to portal vein embolisation: PVE "is frequently used for HCC and colorectal liver metastases and was first described by Makuuchi in 1984 before an extended hepatectomy for bile duct carcinoma."​B&L 69 · p.1212 If you name Makuuchi, name him for PVE.
And the operation that is now standard
B&L: multiple segmentectomies and/or metastectomies is now the standard of care for colorectal liver metastasis.​B&L 69 · p.1211 Not a hemihepatectomy by default, which is the point of departure from SRB's "if secondaries are in a single lobe, hemihepatectomy is done".​SRB 11 · p.605
How wide a margin: one centimetre, or one millimetre? B&L 69 p.1216 calls 1 cm the gold standard and then says 1 mm gives similar survival
The gold standard
"An R0 resection with a negative surgical margin of 1 cm is considered the gold standard."​B&L 69 · p.1216
And the qualification in the same sentence
"...but with effective modern chemotherapy patients with an R1 resection, that is a margin of at least 1 mm microscopically negative, which occurs in 10 to 30% of patients, have similar survivals to those with R0 resections."​B&L 69 · p.1216–1217
Not a contradiction but a shift in what the margin is for, and the correct answer holds both halves. Say: "I would aim for an R0 resection with a 1 cm margin, which remains the gold standard. But a close margin is not a reason to abandon an otherwise feasible resection: an R1 resection with a margin of at least 1 mm that is microscopically negative occurs in 10 to 30% of patients and, with effective modern chemotherapy, gives similar survival."

Why this matters practically: if 1 cm were an absolute requirement, a deposit abutting a major vessel would be inoperable. Because 1 mm suffices, such a deposit can be resected and the patient given systemic therapy. That is the same logic as the whole shift in this chapter, from anatomical rules to functional ones.

Technique, enough to answer the question

How the parenchyma is divided
By CUSA, ultrasonic suction and aspiration, harmonic scalpel or radiofrequency ablation, and B&L is refreshingly honest: it "is a matter of personal preference with no evidence that any method is superior".​B&L 69 · p.1211 Hepatic veins and the Glissonian sheath are now routinely stapled with an endoscopic vascular stapler.​B&L 69 · p.1211
What has made liver surgery safe
"Remarkable progress has been made since the first formal resection in 1952 with the advent of cross-sectional imaging, liver transection technology and low central venous pressure anaesthesia."​B&L 69 · p.1191 The anaesthetic half of that sentence, low central venous pressure, is the part candidates never mention and it is what controls bleeding from the hepatic veins.
And the direction of travel
Laparoscopic and robotic liver surgery, and training with virtual reality.​B&L 69 · p.1191

Non-surgical and palliative options

Chemotherapy, in its proper place
For the 80% not resectable at presentation, and to downstage the 20 to 30% who can be converted.​B&L 69 · p.1216 SRB's position that chemotherapy is the treatment of choice is correct for unresectable disease.​SRB 11 · p.605
Ablation
One of B&L's four tools for increasing the number of potentially curative procedures,​B&L 69 · p.1210 used in combination with resection rather than instead of it.
Blocking the hepatic artery, and the elegant reason it works
SRB's sentence is about ligation, and it is worth quoting as written: "hepatic artery ligation is one of the surgical palliation for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and secondaries in liver as tumour tissue is supplied exclusively by hepatic artery but normal tissue is also supplied by portal vein."​SRB 11 · p.584 That is the whole rationale for every transarterial therapy in the liver, in one sentence: you can starve the tumour because the liver has a second blood supply and the tumour does not.
Ligation and embolisation are not the same wordThe physiology is the same, and SRB does use both, but not in this sentence: p.584 is about ligation, and the guide quoted it under the heading "embolisation". Elsewhere SRB writes "hepatic artery ligation or embolisation is tried"​SRB 21 · p.869 and lists chemoembolisation among the palliative options.​SRB 11 · p.604 So quote ligation for p.584, and say that the same reasoning is what transarterial embolisation rests on.
Dealing with the primary
SRB: if the primary is in the colon, a palliative hemicolectomy is done, and a solitary liver secondary can be resected at the same time.​SRB 11 · p.605 An obstructing or bleeding primary needs treating whatever the liver disease.
And lung metastases are not a bar
Survival after lung resection for colorectal metastases is similar to that after liver resection, 40 to 50%, with low morbidity and mortality.​B&L 69 · p.1217 So a resectable lung deposit alongside resectable liver disease can still be a curative pathway in selected patients.
For completeness: the primary liver tumours in the differential Hepatocellular carcinoma: transplantation by the Milan criteria, first described by Mazzaferro in 1996, that is tumours 5 cm or less, or up to three nodules each 3 cm or less, with angioinvasion and extrahepatic involvement as exclusions; these achieved 4-year overall survival 75% and recurrence-free survival 83% and are now universally accepted, with ablation able to downstage a tumour into the criteria.​B&L 69 · p.1216

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: 20% of cholangiocarcinomas, representing 5 to 30% of primary liver tumours, second only to HCC. Rare in the West at 0.5 to 2 per 100 000, but 60 per 100 000 in Thailand, where Clonorchis sinensis is endemic. Only 30% are suitable for resection at presentation even when confined to the liver, and 5-year survival of 3% remains unchanged.​B&L 69 · p.1216 S Das's reminder that primary carcinoma of the liver is rare and may be a hepatoma or a cholangioma, while secondary carcinoma is much commoner, still holds.​Das 35 · p.524

7Rapid-fire viva

Describe the liver in secondaries.

Enlarged, irregular, hard, with multiple nodules of varying size and shape, the nodules showing central softening and umbilication due to central necrosis.​Das 35 · p.524​SRB 11 · p.605 Add poor general condition, with ascites and jaundice variably present, and the clinical features of the primary. Confirm it is liver by continuity with the liver dullness, movement up and down with respiration, and difficulty moving it sideways.​Das 35 · p.523

Why do the nodules umbilicate?

Central necrosis: the nodule outgrows its blood supply, the centre softens and the surface is drawn in.​SRB 11 · p.605​Das 35 · p.524

By what routes do tumours reach the liver?

Four. Direct spread from stomach, colon, gallbladder and bile ducts. Hepatic artery, classically melanoma. Portal vein, carcinoid and other gastrointestinal malignancies. Lymphatics, breast and lung.​SRB 11 · p.605 S Das puts it as portal vein from the gastrointestinal tract and lymphatics from organs like the breast.​Das 35 · p.524

Synchronous or metachronous?

Synchronous means primary and secondaries found at the same time, typically carcinoma stomach; metachronous means the secondaries appear much later, possibly long after treatment of the primary, typically melanoma and breast.​SRB 11 · p.605 In colorectal cancer, 15 to 25% are synchronous and 20 to 45% metachronous, with up to 70% of patients developing liver metastases overall.​B&L 69 · p.1216

Is this patient curable?

Possibly, and that is the point of the case. Resection remains the only potentially curative option, and five-year survival after resection of liver-only colorectal metastases is about 50%, against under 3% for untreated metastatic disease thirty years ago. Only 20% are resectable at presentation, but a further 20 to 30% become operable after chemotherapy.​B&L 69 · p.1216 So liver-only metastatic colorectal cancer should go to a hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team, not straight to palliation. SRB's position that chemotherapy is the treatment of choice is right for unresectable disease.​SRB 11 · p.605

What makes liver metastases unresectable?

Not number and not size. Resection with curative intent is defined as the ability to remove all residual disease from the liver with clear margins while leaving adequate disease-free viable liver; the technical contraindications are anatomical, chiefly involvement of major vascular or biliary structures. Synchronous disease, a rectal primary, multiple diffuse metastases, a deposit over 5 cm, a disease-free interval under a year and a high CEA were all previously considered contraindications and are not.​B&L 69 · p.1216 Even extrahepatic disease is no longer an absolute bar: long-term survival is possible in selected patients.​B&L 69 · p.1217

How much liver must you leave?

A future liver remnant of at least 25% of total estimated liver volume in a normal liver, and 40% in the presence of cirrhosis; an FLR of 25% of preoperative volume is considered sufficient to prevent postoperative hepatic failure. There is no clear consensus, and those are recommendations rather than absolutes.​B&L 69 · p.1212, p.1217

The remnant would be too small. What can you do?

Grow it. Preoperative portal vein embolisation induces hypertrophy of one side of the liver before resecting the other, increasing the future liver remnant; B&L notes PVE was "first described by Makuuchi in 1984 before an extended hepatectomy for bile duct carcinoma".​B&L 69 · p.1211, p.1212 The other options for converting an inoperable liver are staged resection; ablation; local or multiple segmental resections rather than a hemihepatectomy; and downstaging chemotherapy.​B&L 69 · p.1210, p.1211

What margin do you aim for?

An R0 resection with a 1 cm negative margin is the gold standard. But an R1 resection, meaning a microscopically negative margin of at least 1 mm, occurs in 10 to 30% of patients and, with effective modern chemotherapy, gives similar survival to R0.​B&L 69 · p.1216 So a close margin is not a reason to abandon an otherwise feasible resection.

What is the standard operation for colorectal liver metastases?

Multiple segmentectomies and/or metastectomies, which Bailey and Love calls the standard of care, rather than a hemihepatectomy by default.​B&L 69 · p.1211 This is possible because each segment has its own arterial, portal and biliary supply and its own hepatic vein tributary, which is what makes anatomical segmental resection feasible.​B&L 69 · p.1193

Divide the liver surgically.

At Cantlie's line. Segments V to VIII to the right are supplied by the right hepatic artery and right portal vein and drain by the right hepatic duct; segments I to IV to the left by the left hepatic artery and left portal vein, draining by the left hepatic duct.​B&L 69 · p.1193 Resections of individual segments, of a whole hemiliver, or combinations are all possible.

How would you stage this patient?

Through a specialist multidisciplinary team. Routine staging is triple-phase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis; contrast MRI of the liver; whole-body PET-CT to identify metastatic disease; with or without laparoscopy and intraoperative ultrasonography.​B&L 69 · p.1217 Remember that CT assesses stage and resectability well apart from peritoneal metastases, that MRI is superior for characterising focal liver lesions and small metastases, and that laparoscopy with laparoscopic ultrasound is what finds the small deposits and peritoneal disease the scans missed.​B&L 69 · p.1196​SRB 11 · p.605

You cannot find the primary. How do you look?

Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, contrast radiographs and CT scan,​SRB 11 · p.605 with CEA as a tumour marker. And take the history and examination seriously first: ask about previous cancer surgery such as mastectomy or excision of a melanoma; run SRB's organ checklist for stomach, colon, pancreas and testis; and examine for Troisier's sign and a rectovesical shelf on rectal examination.​SRB 11 · p.605 Liver biopsy is reserved for when the primary cannot be identified by any of these.

Would you biopsy the liver lesion?

Not if I intend to resect it: biopsy should be avoided when surgical resection is being considered, and diagnostic laparoscopy with intraoperative ultrasonography is the better way to resolve doubt.​B&L 69 · p.1216 I would biopsy if the primary cannot be found and the histology will direct chemotherapy, or if the disease is clearly unresectable and tissue is needed before palliative therapy.​SRB 11 · p.605 And before any liver biopsy, exclude hydatid disease, because biopsy will precipitate anaphylaxis; also avoid it in haemangioma, bleeding disorders and ascites.​SRB 11 · p.586

What else gives a nodular liver?

SRB's differential: multicentric hepatoma, macronodular cirrhosis, polycystic liver disease and hydatid cyst of the liver.​SRB 11 · p.605 Add chronic amoebic liver abscess, which gives a smooth, firm or hard, non-tender palpable liver,​SRB 11 · p.590 and remember Riedel's lobe, a congenital tongue-shaped projection from the lower border of the right lobe that is wide and flat and lacks the spherical outline of a distended gallbladder.​Das 35 · p.523

A tender liver with fever and a history of dysentery. What is it and how do you prove it?

Amoebic liver abscess. The patient had amoebic dysentery months or years ago and now has right hypochondrial pain referred to the right shoulder with fever, looks pale and slightly icteric, and has a palpable very tender liver; intercostal tenderness can be elicited even if the liver is not palpable, and the upper limit of liver dullness is raised. Subcutaneous oedema that pits on pressure is an additional finding. On screening the diaphragm is abnormally raised and relatively immobile. Entamoeba histolytica in the stool is diagnostic, and aspiration of anchovy sauce, chocolate-coloured pus leaves no doubt.​Das 35 · p.523 The acute form has high fever, chills and rigors with a soft tender liver; the chronic form a firm or hard, smooth, non-tender liver without acute features.​SRB 11 · p.590

Why does blocking the hepatic artery work?

Because tumour tissue in the liver is supplied exclusively by the hepatic artery, whereas normal liver is also supplied by the portal vein. So embolising the artery starves the tumour while the normal parenchyma survives on its portal supply.​SRB 11 · p.584 It is a palliative option in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and in liver secondaries.

What are the Milan criteria?

Criteria for liver transplantation in hepatocellular carcinoma, first described by Mazzaferro in 1996: tumours 5 cm or less, or up to three nodules each 3 cm or less, with angioinvasion and extrahepatic involvement as additional exclusions. They achieved four-year overall survival of 75% and recurrence-free survival of 83% and are now universally accepted; expanded criteria remain debated, and locoregional therapy such as ablation may downstage a tumour into the criteria, after which transplantation can be considered.​B&L 69 · p.1216

Would lung metastases rule out liver resection?

Not automatically. Extrahepatic metastatic disease was historically a contraindication, but long-term survival is now possible in selected patients, and survival after lung resection for colorectal metastases is similar to that after liver resection, 40 to 50%, with low morbidity and mortality.​B&L 69 · p.1217 It is a decision for a multidisciplinary team, not a rule.

What happens after resection?

Five-year overall survival is about 50%, but tumour recurs in 65%, and in 40% of those the recurrence is limited to the liver.​B&L 69 · p.1216 That last figure matters: because most recurrences are again confined to the liver, re-resection or ablation is often possible, which is one reason these patients need structured follow-up in a specialist unit.

Why is the pain where it is?

Pain in liver secondaries is due to stretching of the liver capsule or to tumour necrosis, and often the pain the patient reports is actually from the primary tumour.​SRB 11 · p.605 So capsular pain tells you the deposits are large or peripheral; it does not tell you they are inoperable.

What has made liver resection safe enough to offer?

Bailey and Love names three things since the first formal resection in 1952: cross-sectional imaging, liver transection technology, and low central venous pressure anaesthesia, which is the one candidates forget and the one that controls hepatic venous bleeding.​B&L 69 · p.1191 Parenchymal division is by CUSA, harmonic scalpel or radiofrequency, and the book is candid that the choice is personal preference with no evidence of superiority; hepatic veins and the Glissonian sheath are now routinely stapled.​B&L 69 · p.1211

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page so they can be found in a different edition. Where the books disagree, both positions are given and the amber boxes say which to answer. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love the liver is chapter 69. This is the case where the three books are furthest apart on management: SRB's account is of a palliative disease with occasional surgery, while the 28th edition treats liver-only colorectal metastasis as potentially curable and has abandoned the number-and-size criteria for resectability altogether. Where they conflict here, the amber boxes side with Bailey & Love, and say why.
